pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Y1). Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, INCLUDING zero (14+5=19, 17−3=14, and the +0/−0 case). The procedural application of within-20 bonds; also where the identity role of zero is established.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including 0'; non-statutory: pupils 'realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5/6 relate counting to addition/subtraction and add/subtract within 20; the additive identity (n+0=n) is an early property.
• Operational details — Use bonds and within-20 strategies to calculate, not counting-all. Give the +0/−0 case explicit attention because young children often assume every operation must change the number — model with objects that adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity unchanged. Keep to the 0-20 range including the teen boundary (crossing ten), reinforcing making-ten. Record with number sentences.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): add/subtract within 20 using bonds or a fast strategy for non-bridging cases (14+5). Tier B (age 5-6): handle bridging cases (8+7) and correctly compute +0/−0. Tier C (age 6): calculate fluently within 20 and explain why adding/subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.
bestPractices: Calculate using known bonds and making-ten rather than counting all, so this procedural work reinforces the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete treatment (adding/taking nothing) to establish zero as the additive identity and dispel 'every operation changes the number'.
Attend to the teen boundary: bridging-ten cases (8+7, 15−7) need the making-ten strategy, not ones-counting.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect to the child's representations to keep meaning attached.
Vary which quantity is unknown lightly to connect with missing-number work.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / rekenrek for within-20 sums and bridging
Empty number line for jumps (including a 0 jump that stays put)
Part-whole model linking the calculation to bonds
Objects demonstrating 'add nothing / take nothing' for the zero case
commonMisconceptions: Assuming +0 or −0 must change the number (giving 5+0=6 or 5−0=4).
Counting all/counting on in ones across the ten boundary instead of making ten.
Errors at the teen boundary (miscounting when crossing 10).
Ignoring the operation and just combining the two numbers seen.
Reversing subtraction to keep the larger number first without noticing the meaning changes.

learn.summary: For ages 5-6 (UK Y1), learners add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers within 20, including the +0/−0 case, using known number bonds and making-ten rather than counting all. Core aims: fluent within-20 calculation, correct bridging across ten (e.g. 8+7), and understanding that adding or subtracting zero leaves a quantity unchanged. Activities centre on acting out calculations with ten-frames and number lines, with a concrete treatment of the zero case to dispel the belief that every operation must change the number.

activities.title: Drive a ten-frame and number-line calculator
feedback: If the learner counts all from one, prompt: hold the first number in mind and count on only the second (hold 14, count on 5 more).
For a bridging case, ask how many more are needed to fill the frame to ten, then how many are left over (8 needs 2 more to make ten, leaving 5, so 15).
If the answer is off by one on the number line, have them name the first jump aloud and check they didn't count the starting number itself as a jump (17 − 3: start at 17, jump back 3 to 14).
activities.rationale: Acting out a calculation on a ten-frame and number line keeps the procedure tied to meaning and reinforces the making-ten strategy at the teen boundary, where ones-counting is error-prone. A live, re-drivable calculation where counters move and a number sentence forms makes the strategy visible; a fixed worked example cannot be re-driven with new numbers.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Build the first number on a double ten-frame (two ten-frames, since one frame holds only 10) (e.g. place eight counters on the first frame for 8+7).

Add or subtract the second number by moving counters, and for bridging cases split the second number to fill the frame to ten first (slide two counters over to complete ten, leaving five, to reach 15).
Show the same calculation as a jump on a 0-20 number line.
Write the matching number sentence alongside the action (e.g. 8 + 7 = 15).
Repeat with a non-bridging case (14 + 5) and a take-away (17 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Within-20 sums and differences can be found by using bonds and making ten, not by counting all in ones; bridging reorganises the quantity around ten.

activities.title: Add nothing, take nothing: the zero case
feedback: If the learner changes the number (e.g. 12 + 0 = 13), act out physically putting zero more counters on, then recount to show the quantity is the same.
Ask directly: when you added nothing, did any counter move? So what is the answer?
Reinforce the contrast: taking 3 away changes the number, taking 0 away does not.
activities.rationale: Young children often assume every operation must change the number, producing errors like 5+0=6 or 5−0=4. Concretely acting out 'add nothing / take nothing' and seeing the quantity unchanged targets this directly and establishes zero's identity role. A side-by-side contrast with a non-zero operation sharpens the point.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
1.OA.5/6: relate counting to add/subtract and add/subtract within 20; the additive identity n + 0 = n is a foundational property.
Y1 pupils add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including 0, and realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0.
learnerActions: Build a number on a double ten-frame (e.g. 12: one full frame and 2 on the second frame).
Choose 'add 0' and watch that no counters move and the number stays 12.
Choose 'subtract 0' from another number (e.g. 16) and confirm it stays 16.
Show the same on the number line as a jump of length zero that stays on the spot.
Say or write why the number did not change: adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity exactly as it was.
Contrast with a nearby case that does change (17 − 3 vs 17 − 0).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 0 leaves a number unchanged (n + 0 = n, n − 0 = n); not every operation changes the quantity.

activities.title: Spoken probe: what happens if we add zero?
feedback: If the explanation is 'it just stays', press for why: because no amount was added or taken away.
Accept correct reasoning expressed in the child's own words; follow a wrong prediction by acting it out with objects.
activities.rationale: A short dialogue may surface the identity idea and let the child articulate reasoning, which the top checkpoint tier expects. Discussion complements, but is not itself calculation practice; the hands-on activities remain the vehicle for building and rehearsing the procedure. Efficacy of the dialogue as a standalone is proposed, not evidenced.
learnerActions: Discuss: 'What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?'
Explain in your own words how 17 − 3 is different from 17 − 0.
Predict and justify the answer to a new zero case before checking it with objects.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state why adding or subtracting zero leaves a number unchanged shows understanding beyond getting the answer.

activities.title: Mixed within-20 practice set
feedback: For an answer like 14 + 5 = 64, show that the 5 ones are added to the 4 ones, not to the ten; make place value visible with tens-and-ones.
For a changed zero answer, re-act adding/taking nothing.
For an off-by-one slip with a sound method, scaffold the count aloud rather than reteaching the strategy.
activities.rationale: Varied practice is needed to build procedural fluency and to probe specific errors (the zero misconception, adding to the wrong part, crossing-ten slips). Including missing-number items lightly connects to later algebraic work. A practice set drills the procedure but relies on the making-ten strategy having been built elsewhere (for example, in the hands-on calculator activity); it does not by itself teach that strategy.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Work a varied set spanning non-bridging sums (14 + 5), bridging sums (8 + 7), take-aways (17 − 3, 15 − 7), and several +0/−0 items (12 + 0, 16 − 0).
Occasionally solve a missing-number item (e.g. 14 + ? = 19) to vary which quantity is unknown.
Jot a number line or ten-frame when helpful.

For non-bridging items, say which digit changed and which stayed the same (14 + 5 → the ones change, 4 + 5 = 9 → 19); notice that in bridging items like 8 + 7 the tens change too, and in ±0 items no digit changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency comes from applying bonds and making-ten across the full 0-20 range, including the zero cases and the teen boundary.

constraints: Keep calculations within the 0-20 range, including the teen boundary (crossing ten).
Use bonds and making-ten rather than counting all; the procedural work should reinforce the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete attention — it is where zero's identity role is established and a common misconception lives.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect them to the child's own representations to keep meaning attached.
A fixed worked example can anchor the ideas but cannot supply the varied, re-drivable practice the procedure needs; use it as an anchor, not the main vehicle.

A practice set drills and assesses the procedure but does not by itself build the making-ten strategy; discussion surfaces reasoning but is not calculation practice. The hands-on calculation is the proposed primary vehicle for building the strategy here, with efficacy stated as proposed rather than proven.

Tiered expectations: at age 5, non-bridging cases via a fast strategy; age 5-6, bridging cases and correct +0/−0; age 6, fluent within-20 calculation with an explanation of why ±0 leaves the number unchanged.

Distinguish subtraction meaning when ordering: 17 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 17; do not reorder subtraction to keep the larger number first without noting the meaning changes (and 3 − 17 lies outside the Y1 within-20 range).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 1.OA.5/6 and the NCETM mastery claim); treat citations accordingly and do not infer tested efficacy.

Self-audit of worked examples: 14 + 5 = 19, 17 − 3 = 14, 8 + 7 = 15, 15 − 7 = 8, 12 + 0 = 12, 16 − 0 = 16, and 14 + ? = 19 → 5 — all checked correct. The diagnostic answer string in the source (19, 14, 12, 16) is consistent.
The source states 14 + 5 'stays within the decade' with 'no crossing of ten'; 14 + 5 = 19 is within the teens with no bridge, so this is correct as stated.

The error-pattern example '14 + 5 given as 64 (added to the tens)' is retained only as a feedback/diagnostic target with corrected framing (ones add to ones); no wrong instruction is presented to the learner.

sourceClaims were trimmed where a cited claim supported only the topic/scope rather than the activity's teaching principle: the DfE scope claim was removed from the ten-frame calculator and mixed-practice activities, and the spoken-probe activity carries no sourceClaims because no source directly supports dialogue efficacy. The DfE claim is retained on the zero-case activity because it explicitly includes 'realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0'.

Medium-superiority language was softened: the practice set's reliance on prior strategy-building is scoped to 'elsewhere' rather than asserting hands-on is the only route, and 'Neither replaces hands-on calculation' was reworded to a proposed primary vehicle, consistent with the untested efficacy of the specific interaction.
The 3D/spatial 'skip' framing was dropped as a catalog judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; within-20 calculation is simply better served by the ten-frame/number-line medium here.

probeDeeper: For 14 + 5, which digit changes and which stays the same? Why?
What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?
Show me on the number line how you got 19.
assess.correctAnswer: 19, 14, 12, 16 — the first two stay within the decade (add/subtract to the ones), and adding or subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts to the wrong part, or counts all from one instead of counting on from 14.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use tens-and-ones or a number line — hold 14, count on 5, adding ones to the ones; make the place value visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 14 + 5 given as e.g. 64 (added to the tens) or laboriously counted from one.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Act out adding nothing / taking nothing away to establish that zero leaves the quantity unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child alters the number when adding or subtracting zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Method right but counting-on/back slips by one (off-by-one).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold count-back, naming the first jump aloud; the strategy is sound, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 17 − 3 given as 15 (counted the starting number as the first jump).

responseLevels.gap: Adds to the wrong part, counts all from one, or changes the number when adding/subtracting zero.
responseLevels.full: Adds/subtracts ones within the teens by place value, counting on/back efficiently, and treats ± 0 as leaving the number unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates within the decade correctly but slowly by counting, or is unsure about the zero cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out (you can jot or use a number line): 14 + 5? … 17 − 3? … 12 + 0? … 16 − 0?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These stay within the teens with no crossing of ten, so a child who understands place value adds the ones to the ones digit (14 + 5 → 4 + 5 = 9 → 19). Watch for adding to the wrong part or counting all from one; the ± 0 items catch the belief that an operation must change the number.
